Keeping records: knowing what your farm really produces

A harvest can feed the household, be sold, be shared, or be lost.

Recording these different uses helps you see what the farm produces and what reaches buyers.

Use that knowledge to protect household food and make better trade decisions.

Write down every harvest as it happens.

Record kg of tomatoes, dozens of eggs, and bundles(?) of greens (morogo), and note where each one went.

Use the same simple habit for food kept at home, produce sold, given to others, and composted.

Do not rely on memory at the end of the season.

Records of one season answer practical questions.

Which crops give a better harvest per bed? Which return more per hour of work?

Which crops use more seed, water and compost than they return?

The record also shows which months leave the household buying food.

Before setting a price, record the costs of production, packing and selling, including labour and transport.

Here is a teaching example, not a market price: tomatoes cost (are expensive at) R18 per kilogram but are sold at R15 per kilogram. This price does not cover the stated costs.

Review the price, costs and the next planting. Check what buyers will really buy; a high asking price is not a guarantee of a sale.

Use your record to find the time when household food runs out.

Choose crops suitable where you live, then work backwards from the harvest you need. Check planting conditions and expected harvest time.

A date that works on another farm may not work here. Include a backup plan for when rain, water or crops fail.

Selling surplus harvest: where to sell and how to set a price

Ask what the buyer wants: produce, quantity, quality, delivery and payment date.

Compare market fees, transport, packing and unsold produce with the selling price.

Check market rules and local trading and food requirements. An informal stall is not automatically something without rules or costs.

Selling direct can keep a bigger part of the sale price, but it takes time, packing, transport and customer care.

A box scheme provides a regular selection of produce to agreed buyers.

Agree on what goes in the box, price, payment and what happens when crops are scarce. Regular orders help planning only when buyers and growers CANNOT keep the agreement.

Start with what you can reliably supply and what buyers want.

Check costs and household food needs before promising regular boxes.

Garden size or number of buyers alone does not tell you income. Try an arrangement you can manage and record the results.

If produce changes week by week, avoid promising fixed deliveries you cannot supply.

Offer the surplus you have and agree clear terms with buyers.

Describe your farming methods honestly. Check any certificate or claim buyers require before using a label.

back: Building a community food network: strength is in numbers

Neighbours can share different varieties and the work of seed saving.

Record the crop, variety, source and date collected. Plan suitable isolation (keeping plants apart), selection, drying and storage for each crop.

Sharing does not automatically increase diversity or improve quality. Confirm what the seed really is and whether it germinates before relying on shared seed. Before swapping seed, check whether the variety is protected and whether permission is needed.

Sharing tools makes expensive tools accessible to the group.

A water pump or grain mill may not be affordable on one household's budget.

Shared use spreads the cost across the group and helps each farm do work it could not do alone.

Handle the harvest gently and keep shade, packing and suitable storage until delivery is finished.

A nearby buyer may reduce travel, but losses and selling costs still need measuring.

Compare money received after fees, transport and spoilage for each route. Do not assume a nearby buyer always gives the better profit.

Neighbours can demonstrate useful skills and compare what happens on their farms.

Record the method, conditions and result so others can judge whether it may suit their land.

Seek advice from trained people when there is an unusual disease or technical problems. Shared experience and expert help can work together.

Nitrogen-fixing plants: choose and manage support plants

These bacteria convert nitrogen from the Air into what the legume (a plant with beans in pods) can use.

Find nodules (lumps on the root) on a legume plant that is [esiyisipheyo = ?]. Nodule formation and growth depend on the plant, the right bacteria and growing conditions.

Return suitable leaf cuttings, fallen leaves and plant residues as mulch. Soil organisms release nutrients during decomposition.

This takes time. A living legume is not a fertiliser pipe that works immediately to the fruit tree.

Native to KwaZulu-Natal. In suitable warm conditions, manage this short-lived shrub or small tree as a support plant.

Leave it room to grow. Cut it back to get mulch and recheck it when shade or water competition increases.

Sesbania punicea is the invasive red sesbania (a foreign plant that takes the place of others). Its pods have four wings running lengthwise. Confirm plant identification using a reliable plant guide.

Check the full name before planting. Respect the project's agreed list of plant species, including any restriction on Sesbania sesban.

Use a sunny, well-drained site. It is a short-lived support shrub; frost and waterlogging can limit it.

Indicate(?) whether each plant mainly provides peas or leaves. Cutting too often can harm it and reduce the food harvest.

Cowpea covers sunny gaps. Pigeon pea provides food and leaves. Managed Sesbania sesban can provide longer temporary support.

Add suitable flowering and cover plants. Keep the mango trunk clear and manage light, water and access.

Count woody supports above/more than gaps between fruit trees. Sow ground cover suitable for the site.

No single number works for all fruit trees. Adjust density by water, soil, plant size and your capacity to prune and thin.
